broad.question: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that trace boron enhances the formation of beneficial, fine TiB2 particles (as in the paper) and its relation to improved hardness and wear resistance, extending that concept to explain simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance through passive film stabilization.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It explicitly links the nanoscale dispersion of in situ ceramic precipitates with dual performance against wear and corrosion, proposing that a uniform ultrafine particle distribution under controlled boron addition enhances the adhesion and stability of the passive film, a mechanism not specifically isolated in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Optimizing the nanoscale dispersion and size of in situ TiB2 particles in the HEA coating governs simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance by promoting grain refinement that impedes dislocation motion and providing abundant, uniformly distributed nucleation sites for a coherent passive film that resists localized breakdown.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coating produced by laser cladding with no or excessive boron addition, leading to either coarse or inhomogeneously distributed TiB2.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a precisely controlled, trace amount of boron (near x = 0.5) during laser cladding to yield a uniform dispersion of ultrafine TiB2 precipitates.
hypothesis.conditions: Coatings are produced under identical laser cladding parameters, with only the boron content adjusted to target ultrafine particle formation in a harsh corrosive mechanical environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl with imposed sliding wear).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A significantly refined and homogeneous microstructure with nanoscale TiB2 precipitates and smaller BCC grain sizes.
hypothesis.mechanism: The ultrafine TiB2 particles act as barriers to dislocation motion (enhancing wear resistance by impeding plastic deformation) and serve as effective nucleation sites for stable, adherent passive films (reducing localized corrosion initiation). The refined grains further contribute by creating more grain boundaries that can slow corrosion pathways and impede crack propagation under cyclic mechanical loading.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline with either no B or excessive B (leading to coarse TiB2), the optimized coating will exhibit a significantly lower wear rate (potentially reduced by similar orders as S2–S3 in the paper) and a lower corrosion current density (with icorr reduced by around 50% relative to non-optimized coatings).
hypothesis.baseline: Coatings produced with either no boron (coarser microstructure) or with excessive boron resulting in agglomerated TiB2 which promotes stress concentration and defective passive films.
hypothesis.boundary: This prediction should hold when the processing parameters ensure full melting/solidification control and homogeneity; however, if the laser cladding process introduces other uncontrolled defects or if the aggressive environment exceeds the stability limits of the passive film, the benefit may be diminished.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in wear rate and corrosion current is uncertain, though the trend is expected to follow the comparative improvements seen in the optimized S2–S3 compositions reported in the paper.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings by laser cladding: one with the controlled low boron content aimed at ultrafine TiB2 particle formation (optimized condition) and one with no boron (baseline). Subject both sets to simultaneous cyclic wear (using a tribometer under controlled load) and corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt.% NaCl).
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/N·m)
Coefficient of friction (COF)
Corrosion current density (icorr)
Microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS and XRD to assess particle size/distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized coating does not show a statistically significant improvement in both wear rate and corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or worse icorr and wear rate than the baseline), or if microstructural analysis shows no difference in TiB2 dispersion, the hypothesis would be falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: Leverages the paper's demonstration of grain refinement and dynamic amorphization under sliding while introducing controlled cyclic loading to optimize the trade-off between wear-induced nanocrystallization and time-dependent recrystallization/passivation in corrosive settings.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a programmable sliding regimen to dynamically maintain an optimal ultra-nanocrystalline state that enhances both mechanical and chemical resilience, directly linking shear rate programming with concurrent improvements in corrosion resistance.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by a dynamic balance between grain refinement and limited recrystallization in the surface layer, such that continuous cyclic shear maintains an optimal ultra-nanocrystalline state that promotes rapid surface passivation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA produced through additive manufacturing with initially large grains (~42 µm) that undergo severe shear-induced grain refinement during sliding.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement a programmed sliding regimen with carefully timed cycle durations and pause intervals in a corrosive (chloride-rich) environment to regulate the balance between dynamic nanocrystallization and recrystallization of the surface layer.
hypothesis.conditions: Tribocorrosion experiments at ambient temperature in a chloride electrolyte where sliding cycles (and intermittent stops) are varied to modulate the extent of grain refinement versus time-dependent grain growth (recrystallization) and passivation film repair.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A continuously renewed ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer (grain sizes in the 2–10 nm range) that maintains high concentrations of active grain boundaries, which enable both low friction (via inverse Hall-Petch mechanisms) and rapid formation of protective oxide patches.
hypothesis.mechanism: During cyclic sliding, the surface evolves through rapid grain refinement due to high shear, which lowers friction through inverse Hall-Petch softening. However, pauses allow limited recrystallization and grain growth, which can temporarily increase the surface hardness. In a corrosive environment, freshly exposed high-energy grain boundaries rapidly form oxide passivation patches. By programming the cycle duration, the dynamic equilibrium can be tuned to favor a persistently refined, passivated surface that resists both mechanical wear and corrosive attack.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline sample having a continuous, unmodulated sliding regimen (e.g., constant cycling without pauses or with excessively long pause times), the optimized cycling condition will display lower steady-state friction, reduced wear rates, and decreased corrosion current densities. The improvements should be evident at moderate loads where the dynamic balance can be maintained.
hypothesis.baseline: A control HEA sample tested under continuous sliding without controlled pause intervals, leading either to excessive grain growth (diminishing rapid passivation) or poorly managed wear rates.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under conditions where the time scales for shear-induced grain refinement and thermally driven recrystallization are suitably separated. If pauses are too long (allowing extensive grain growth) or if the sliding cycle is too aggressive (preventing oxide repair), the protective effect may fail.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise interplay between cycling time, grain refinement kinetics, and passivation dynamics in a corrosive environment is complex, and the optimal timing parameters require careful calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple groups of HEA samples subjected to tribocorrosion tests under different programmed sliding regimens—for example, continuous sliding versus controlled cycling with varied pause durations. Characterize the surface microstructure (grain size distribution via TEM), passivation quality (using XPS), and record friction, wear, and corrosion data.
measurements: Surface grain size distributions (TEM)
Thickness and quality of oxide passivation (XPS)
Steady-state friction coefficients
Wear volume (profilometry)
Corrosion current densities (electrochemical tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples under optimized cyclic sliding do not show a statistically significant improvement in maintaining an ultra-nanocrystalline, passivated surface along with reduced wear and corrosion compared to the continuous sliding baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C14

source_paper.title: Mechanical and Corrosion Behavior of Zr-Doped High-Entropy Alloy from CoCrFeMoNi System.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding in PMC10003814 that the passive film characteristics are crucial for corrosion resistance and the metallurgical principle that grain refinement and compressive stress can enhance film repair (TXT::wikipedia::Crystallographic_texture::006)
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis decouples alloy composition from wear–corrosion performance by introducing a physical surface modification process that creates a beneficial gradient microstructure rather than relying on chemical doping (e.g., with Zr), which in the paper led to mixed effects.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Introducing a surface gradient microstructure via a non-chemical process will enhance simultaneous wear–corrosion resistance by promoting rapid repassivation and ameliorating stress concentrations at the surface.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A conventional cast and homogenized CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy with a uniform, relatively coarse microstructure.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a surface treatment such as laser shock peening or controlled surface remelting to generate a nanolaminated (graded) microstructure confined to the top few microns without altering the bulk composition.
hypothesis.conditions: Expose both the surface-modified and unmodified samples to an environment simulating harsh conditions, e.g., cyclic sliding wear tests combined with immersion in 3.5% NaCl solution.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A gradient microstructure with ultrafine grains and compressive residual stresses at the surface is expected to enhance the kinetics of passive film formation and repair while reducing the initiation of micro-cracks under mechanical loads.
hypothesis.mechanism: The refined surface layer, with higher grain boundary density and compressive stresses, accelerates re-passivation following mechanical removal of oxides; simultaneously, it distributes stress more uniformly to reduce local damage, thereby mitigating wear-induced interruption of the protective film. This dynamic equilibrium between film removal and rapid self-repair governs the combined degradation resistance.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The surface-modified HEA is predicted to exhibit lower wear rates and lower corrosion current density (indicating improved passive film performance) under combined mechanical and corrosive loading compared to the untreated baseline. The improvement is expected to be moderate but significant under typical ambient conditions.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-cast, uniformly microstructured CoCrFeNiMo alloy with a passive film that does not benefit from induced compressive stresses or a nanolaminate gradient.
hypothesis.boundary: This enhanced performance is likely to persist under moderate to severe cyclic loading and corrosion; however, in extreme conditions (excessive impact or very low temperatures where diffusion is limited) the protective effect may be diminished.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the trend is supported by principles of compressive surface treatments and grain-boundary–mediated repassivation, the precise magnitude of improvement remains uncertain due to potential scale effects in the surface layer.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNiMo HEA samples: one set subjected to laser shock peening to produce a nanolaminated gradient layer, and an untreated control. Subject both sets to identical cyclic sliding wear tests while immersed in 3.5% NaCl solution, monitoring electrochemical potential and wear depth.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess passive film quality
Wear volume loss (using profilometry)
Surface residual stress (e.g., XRD stress measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not show statistically significant lower wear loss and decreased corrosion rates (or fail to demonstrate a more rapid reformation of the passive film) in comparison with the untreated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C11

source_paper.title: Study on Microstructures and Properties of FeCoNiCuAlSi<sub>x</sub> High-Entropy Alloy Composite Coatings by Laser Cladding.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s observation that Si addition improves corrosion resistance (via enhanced passivation and microstructural refinement) and builds on the concept of self-healing oxide films known from galvanic corrosion studies (TXT::wikipedia::Galvanic_corrosion::015).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This approach explicitly leverages post-processing heat treatment to enhance elemental segregation at grain boundaries, thereby promoting a self-healing passive layer—a nuanced mechanism for simultaneous wear and corrosion protection that goes beyond the as-clad microstructural modifications explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The resistance of high-entropy alloys to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by the localized self-passivation phenomenon resulting from the preferential segregation of silicon (and associated aluminum) at grain boundaries during rapid solidification, which forms a continuous, self-healing oxide layer that protects against both mechanical wear and chemical attack.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A rapidly solidified FeCoNiCuAl-based high-entropy alloy coating produced by laser cladding in a conventional setup, without post-processing to enhance surface segregation.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a short post-cladding heat treatment in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere to promote further segregation of Si (and Al) to the grain boundaries, facilitating the formation of a thin, adherent oxide film (comprising Al2O3/SiO2).
hypothesis.conditions: Evaluation under combined tribocorrosion conditions: cyclic mechanical sliding under moderate load in NS4 solution at controlled ambient or slightly elevated temperatures.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries enriched in Si/Al that act as sites for continuous passive film formation.
hypothesis.mechanism: During rapid solidification, Si atoms already influence the microstructure by favoring a BCC formation. The heat treatment in an oxidizing atmosphere further drives the segregation of Si (and mobilized Al) to the grain boundaries. These enriched boundaries then oxidize to form a thin, self-healing passive film that can repair minor mechanical damage in situ. This dynamic film not only minimizes localized corrosion at high-energy boundary regions but also reduces the direct metal-on-metal contact during sliding, thus decreasing wear.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated HEA coatings, the post-treated samples should exhibit lower corrosion current densities and improved wear rates. In combined tests, the post-treated samples should maintain lower mass loss and a more stable (and lower) friction coefficient, particularly under conditions where damage to the passive film is expected in untreated samples.
hypothesis.baseline: As-clad HEA coatings with typical Si segregation levels and without post-cladding heat treatment.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is most effective when the heat treatment provides sufficient thermal activation for elemental segregation without causing coarsening or other deleterious phase transformations. Under extreme thermal or mechanical conditions where the passive film is repeatedly disrupted beyond self-healing capacity, the benefit may not persist.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The rate of self-healing and the durability of the passivation film under cyclic deleterious conditions have uncertainty; quantification of film healing kinetics under dynamic wear remains to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings by laser cladding. Subject one set to a short post-cladding heat treatment in a controlled oxidizing atmosphere to induce enhanced Si/Al segregation, while leaving the other set as-clad. Expose both sets to cyclic tribocorrosion testing in NS4 solution at similar loads and temperatures.
measurements: Surface and grain boundary composition analysis (EDS, XPS) before and after testing
Electrochemical measurements (Tafel curves, EIS) to assess passivation quality
Wear track depth and mass loss measurements
Friction coefficient monitoring during cyclic sliding
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-treated samples do not exhibit a consistently lower combined wear-corrosion rate and no evidence of enhanced grain boundary segregation or continuous passive film compared to the as-clad baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

hypotheses.label: C9

source_paper.title: A Lightweight AlTiVNb High-Entropy Alloy Film with High Strength-Ductility Synergy and Corrosion Resistance.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observation of island structures and nanovoids in the amorphous HEA film from PMC9735962, combined with principles of void collapse enhancing local densification and passivation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely links the intrinsic, engineered nanovoid population—and its collapse under mechanical load—to enhanced oxide layer densification, thereby providing a mechanistic explanation for simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance in high-entropy alloys.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The collapse and densification of intrinsic nanovoids within the island-structured amorphous HEA under mechanical wear locally enhances oxide film integrity, thereby minimizing pathways for corrosive attack.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An amorphous AlTiVNb HEA film with an island microstructure exhibiting intrinsic small-scale voids and homogeneous chemical disorder as described in PMC9735962.
hypothesis.intervention: Tailor the deposition parameters (e.g., modify sputtering pressure or substrate bias) to systematically vary the size and density of the intrinsic nanovoids without crystallizing the film.
hypothesis.conditions: Prepare two sets of films: one with the baseline void characteristics and a second with a higher density of finely distributed nanovoids engineered via altered deposition parameters. Subject both to simultaneous wear-corrosion testing in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under identical sliding load conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The engineered nanovoids act as zones that collapse under mechanical load, thereby densifying the near-surface region and facilitating rapid repassivation by shortening diffusion paths for oxygen.
hypothesis.mechanism: During wear, the localized mechanical energy causes the pre-existing nanovoids (formed via the coalescence-induced void formation mechanism) to collapse. This densification suppresses the formation and propagation of microcracks in the oxide film. The resulting compact oxide minimizes penetration of corrosive species, reducing both wear-induced damage and corrosion attack.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The films with a higher density of fine nanovoids, which collapse to densify the surface under load, are expected to show lower wear volumes and reduced corrosion current densities compared to the baseline film. The improvement should be apparent under moderate wear loads; if the void density is too high or too low, the effect may weaken.
hypothesis.baseline: The standard as-deposited homogeneous amorphous AlTiVNb film with its initial island and void structure as reported in the paper.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is effective only if the void characteristics remain within an optimal range. Excessively high void volume could lead to premature failure, while too low a density might not provide the necessary densification effect.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise control of void collapse dynamics and its quantitative impact on oxide film repair remains to be exactly determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two series of films with distinct void populations (baseline and modified via adjusted sputtering parameters). Perform combined sliding wear tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution and assess the surface densification post-wear using cross-sectional TEM and XPS, along with corrosion Tafel analysis and wear volume measurements.
measurements: Characterize void collapse and oxide layer compactness via cross-sectional TEM/XPS.
Measure corrosion current density via Tafel polarization testing.
Quantify wear depth and track volume using profilometry or SEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the films engineered for increased nanovoid density do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxide integrity, and if their corresponding wear and corrosion metrics are not better than the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C13

source_paper.title: Microstructural, Mechanical, and Electrochemical Characterization of CrMoNbTiZr High-Entropy Alloy for Biomedical Application.

hypotheses.builds_on: general concepts from materials science on the role of grain boundaries in both mechanical strengthening and enhanced oxygen diffusion for passive film formation, applied here specifically to the CrMoNbTiZr HEA system as characterized in the paper.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It specifically tailors the grain boundary density through controlled thermomechanical processing to achieve a balance between enhanced passivation kinetics and mechanical resistance against wear—a variable not addressed in the original SPS processing study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Optimal grain boundary engineering via moderate thermomechanical processing governs simultaneous wear–corrosion resistance by enhancing passive film formation kinetics while maintaining mechanical integrity.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An SPS-produced CrMoNbTiZr HEA with a relatively coarse grain structure and moderate grain boundary density.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a controlled thermomechanical processing route (e.g., moderate equal channel angular pressing followed by an annealing step) to refine the grain size to an intermediate regime—finer than the baseline but not so fine as to invite excessive intergranular corrosion.
hypothesis.conditions: Subject both the refined-grained and baseline HEA samples to simultaneous wear–corrosion tests in a chloride-containing solution (such as Hanks’ or PBS) at room temperature under controlled sliding wear conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An increased, yet optimal, density of grain boundaries that serve as rapid diffusion pathways for oxygen and other oxidizing species, promoting fast reformation of a protective passive film after wear-induced disruption.
hypothesis.mechanism: Grain boundaries can act as sites for accelerated oxide formation due to high diffusivity and reactive sites. In the optimal grain size regime, the higher grain boundary density aids in quick repassivation to heal wear damage; simultaneously, the moderate refinement provides improved hardness to resist wear. However, avoiding extreme nanocrystallinity prevents the deleterious effects of excessive intergranular corrosion.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The thermomechanically processed HEA with optimized grain size should exhibit lower combined wear and corrosion damage—reflected in reduced wear volume and lower corrosion current densities—compared to the coarser-grained baseline.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-sintered CrMoNbTiZr HEA possessing a coarse grain structure as produced by SPS.
hypothesis.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold at room temperature and under moderate mechanical loads where diffusion-mediated passive film formation is effective; however, if the processing over-refines the grain structure or if the testing environment imposes aggressive intergranular attack conditions (e.g., high temperatures), the benefit might be negated.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise quantitative impact of grain size reduction on tribocorrosion performance in this HEA system is uncertain without a dedicated parametric study, though the qualitative trend is supported by established materials principles (KG::grain_size::dcc069dcf5, KG::grains_boundary::ff7e991aa2).

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA samples: one retaining the coarse-grained structure from SPS and another processed via moderate thermomechanical deformation to achieve the target intermediate grain size. Subject both sets to identical tribocorrosion tests in a chloride-based solution.
measurements: Grain size distribution analysis (via SEM/EBSD)
Wear track profiling (measuring wear volume and scar depth)
Electrochemical testing (Tafel analysis to determine corrosion current density)
Passive film characterization (XPS or similar surface analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined-grained samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in both mechanical wear resistance and corrosion rate (i.e., faster reformation and more uniform passive film) compared to the coarse-grained baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observation in the paper that excessive or loosely bonded TiB2 particles can lead to spalling and galvanic corrosion, transforming that finding into a targeted interfacial engineering approach.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a novel post-processing heat treatment to enhance not just the microstructure but specifically the particle–matrix interfaces, thereby simultaneously mitigating wear and corrosion mechanisms—a factor that the paper identified as a detriment when TiB2 particles are oversized or agglomerated but did not address with heat treatment.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Enhancing the interfacial bonding between in situ formed TiB2 particles and the HEA matrix via tailored post-cladding heat treatment governs the resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion by mitigating stress concentrations and reducing galvanic coupling at particle–matrix interfaces.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy coating with in situ formed TiB2 particles produced by laser cladding, which in its as-cladded state may exhibit suboptimal particle–matrix bonding and localized defects.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a post-laser cladding annealing treatment (at a temperature below the primary melting point but high enough to improve interfacial diffusion) aimed at enhancing metallurgical bonding between TiB2 reinforcements and the HEA matrix.
hypothesis.conditions: Maintain constant cladding parameters and composition, comparing as-cladded coatings (baseline) with annealed coatings, while testing both under combined wear-corrosion conditions (e.g., sliding wear in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Improved interfacial bonding with reduced micro-scale gaps and minimized stress-concentrated sites at the TiB2/matrix interfaces.
hypothesis.mechanism: Enhanced bonding reduces the likelihood of particle detachment that normally acts as stress concentrators leading to spalling during wear, and it minimizes the formation of micro-galvanic cells that accelerate localized corrosion. The improved interface provides a continuous load-transfer path and a more uniform distribution of mechanical stress and electrochemical potential.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Annealed coatings will display reduced adhesive wear (with fewer spalling events) and lower corrosion rates (evidenced by lower icorr and improved passivation film stability) when compared to the as-cladded baseline.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-cladded HEA coating with in situ formed TiB2 particles, which may suffer from weak particle–matrix bonding and associated degradation under combined mechanical and corrosive stresses.
hypothesis.boundary: The heat treatment must be controlled such that it does not coarsen the grain structure excessively or degrade the beneficial dispersion of TiB2. In environments where heat-induced phase transformations occur or where the annealing atmosphere is not controlled, the benefit may be negated.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement in interfacial bonding is expected to lower wear and corrosion degradation, the precise extent of reduction in degradation rates is uncertain due to process sensitivity.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two batches of HEA coatings with identical initial composition via laser cladding. Subject one batch to an optimized post-cladding annealing treatment and keep the other as-cladded. Perform mechanical wear tests combined with electrochemical corrosion measurements (potentiodynamic polarization, EIS) in a corrosive medium under sliding conditions.
measurements: Interfacial integrity (observed with high-resolution SEM/TEM)
Wear rate and spalling incidence
Corrosion current density (icorr) and passivation film characteristics via EIS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed coatings do not show a significant improvement in both wear and corrosion performance (or if microstructural analysis shows no improvement in interfacial bonding), the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C7

source_paper.title: Erosion and Corrosion Resistance Performance of Laser Metal Deposited High-Entropy Alloy Coatings at Hellisheidi Geothermal Site.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation that manufacturing cracks (PMC8200011::web::003, PMC8200011::web::015) promote local erosion-corrosion damage via enhanced fluid turbulence and galvanic effects.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes an active post-processing treatment to heal inherent deposition defects to yield a mechanically robust oxide film under simultaneous erosive and corrosive stresses—a concept not examined in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Eliminating processing‐induced defects (especially cracks) enables the formation of a continuous, mechanically robust passive oxide film on HEA surfaces which governs simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: LMD-deposited CoCrFeNiMo0.85 HEA coatings that as-deposited on carbon steel or stainless steel substrates may contain manufacturing cracks/porosity.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a post-deposition annealing or hot isostatic pressing (HIP) step to heal cracks and reduce residual stresses in the HEA coating.
hypothesis.conditions: Test in simulated geothermal fluid environments (deaerated and aerated conditions) with superimposed mechanical erosive impacts; perform comparisons between as-deposited and annealed/HIP-treated samples.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The integrity of the passive Cr-O-rich oxide film formed on the HEA surface.
hypothesis.mechanism: By reducing manufacturing defects, stress concentrations that lead to film rupture or discontinuous oxide layers are minimized. A continuous passive oxide film (observed in aerated tests in Mo-HEA coatings on stainless steel, e.g., PMC8200011::web::009 and PMC8200011::web::019) acts as both a corrosion barrier and a mechanical buffer, reducing the initiation sites for erosive wear. The improved adhesion and continuity mitigate the synergistic effects where microcracks accelerate material removal.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The annealed/HIP-treated HEA samples will exhibit a lower combined degradation rate (both wear and corrosion) compared to as-deposited samples, with a measurable improvement (uncertain magnitude) in passive film continuity and coating thickness retention.
hypothesis.baseline: As-deposited LMD HEA coatings that show manufacturing cracks and discontinuous passive films (e.g., Mo-HEA on carbon steel, as reported in PMC8200011::web::003 and PMC8200011::web::015).
hypothesis.boundary: The protective effect should be significant under moderate erosive conditions and in fluids where passive film formation is operative; however, at extreme mechanical impacts or highly aggressive chemical conditions, the benefit may diminish.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement is uncertain, as the exact relationship between defect healing and passive film stability under cyclic erosion-corrosion remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA-coated samples on the same substrate: one set as-deposited and one subjected to post-deposition annealing/HIP. Expose both sets to identical simulated geothermal conditions with a standardized mechanical erosion apparatus.
measurements: Surface morphology and continuity of the oxide film (via SEM/BSE/EDS)
Coating thickness before and after exposure (optical profilometry)
Weight loss or pit depth analysis as a measure of combined degradation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed/HIP-treated samples do not show statistically significant reduction in wear-corrosion degradation (no improvement in oxide continuity or damage metrics) compared to the as-deposited samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: Study on Microstructures and Properties of FeCoNiCuAlSi<sub>x</sub> High-Entropy Alloy Composite Coatings by Laser Cladding.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s finding that Si addition enhances hardness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance (via phase transformation and passivation) in FeCoNiCuAlSi coatings.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s observations to harsh, simultaneous wear-corrosion environments by directly linking microstructural refinement and dual-phase formation (FCC+BCC) to the dual protection mechanism—mechanical load-bearing and passive film stability—thus providing a single unified mechanistic explanation.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance is governed by a synergistic effect of microstructural refinement and phase transformation—specifically, the formation of a dual-phase (FCC+BCC) microstructure with a high BCC fraction induced by silicon addition—that enhances hardness (thus reducing abrasive wear) and promotes the development of a stable, adherent passivation film (e.g., Al2O3) along the refined grain boundaries.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A FeCoNiCuAl-based high-entropy alloy coating with a predominantly FCC matrix and coarse grains.
hypothesis.intervention: Incorporate silicon at increased levels (targeting a composition similar to FeCoNiCuAlSi2.0) during laser cladding to promote BCC phase formation, refine the dendritic microstructure, and enhance hardness.
hypothesis.conditions: Testing in NS4 solution to simulate corrosive soil pore water plus mechanical wear under controlled sliding conditions (e.g., constant load tribometer tests).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Refined grain structure and increased BCC phase fraction with enriched grain boundary sites for passivation film nucleation.
hypothesis.mechanism: The increased Si content induces lattice distortion and accelerates the FCC-to-BCC transformation. The fine, dense dendritic structure restricts dislocation motion (enhancing hardness and wear resistance), while the uniformly distributed grain boundaries become preferential sites for the formation of a protective Al2O3 passive film. The passive film reduces anodic reaction rates during corrosion and together with high hardness, resists the mechanical removal of the film during sliding wear.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy without Si, the Si-enhanced coating should exhibit a ~50–60% increase in microhardness and a significant reduction in both wear rate and corrosion current density. Under combined wear-corrosion testing, the degradation should be markedly lower due to the stable passive film and enhanced hardness.
hypothesis.baseline: FeCoNiCuAl high-entropy alloy coating without added silicon (or with minimal Si content).
hypothesis.boundary: The prediction should hold under conditions where the environment is moderately acidic/basic (NS4 solution) and mechanical stresses remain within the elastic to early plastic deformation regime. At extremely high mechanical loads or severe chemical attack exceeding the passive film stability, the benefit may diminish.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in combined degradation rates may vary; further testing is needed to delineate load thresholds and chemical extremes.

Monitor both the wear volume and the corrosion current (using electrochemical measurements) over time.
measurements: Wear volume via white-light interferometry
Corrosion current density via potentiodynamic polarization
Surface oxide integrity via SEM/EDS mapping
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized alloy (with reduced interphase potential differences) does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in coupled degradation—i.e., similar wear and corrosion rates as the standard alloy—the hypothesis that galvanic coupling from oxide film breakdown is the primary accelerator is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C2

source_paper.title: Influence of Laser Power on CoCrFeNiMo High-Entropy Alloy Coating Microstructure and Properties.

hypotheses.builds_on: The observed formation of microcracks and poor interfacial integrity at high laser power attributed to thermal stresses (PMC12156342::web::016::3_1_phase_composition_and_microstructure) combined with principles of thermally induced fatigue in multiphase materials (TXT::wikipedia::High-temperature_corrosion::014).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces cyclic thermal expansion mismatch as a key driver of microcracking and coupled degradation in a multi-phase HEA under wear – a mechanism distinct from purely galvanic or compositional change effects discussed in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation is driven by thermomechanical fatigue arising from cyclic thermal expansion mismatch between the FCC and σ phases under elevated temperature, which is further amplified by wear; the cyclic stress causes microcracking and spallation at phase boundaries, thereby exposing fresh surfaces to aggressive corrosion, and the resulting pits act as stress concentrators that enhance wear.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy with inherently different coefficients of thermal expansion between the FCC matrix and the harder σ phase.
hypothesis.intervention: Design a controlled study that adjusts the residual thermal stresses via a post-deposition heat treatment (e.g., a subcritical anneal) aimed at reducing the thermal mismatch between phases. Compare the mechanically polished as-clad HEA with the post-treated HEA.
hypothesis.conditions: Exposure to high temperatures (e.g., 600–700 °C) and cyclic thermal loading combined with continuous sliding wear in a corrosive environment, conditions under which differential thermal expansion becomes significant.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The phase boundaries between the FCC and σ phases and the residual interlayer stresses built during rapid processing.
hypothesis.mechanism: Under cyclic heating (or sustained elevated temperature coupled with mechanical frictional heating), the mismatch in thermal expansion between the FCC and σ phases generates cyclic stresses at their interfaces. These stresses initiate microcracks along the phase boundaries. The concurrent wear process then exacerbates these microcracks by mechanically removing loosely attached fragments. The microcracks expose fresh metal to the corrosive environment, leading to accelerated corrosion (especially galvanic in nature given the phase differences). The cumulative effect of microcracking, wear-induced spallation, and accelerated localized corrosion results in coupled degradation that is significantly more rapid than the sum of the individual effects.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The as-clad alloys with higher residual thermal stresses and pronounced thermal expansion mismatch will show a higher degradation rate, with increased microcrack density, spallation, and higher corrosion currents compared to the post-heat-treated, stress-relieved samples. Total degradation is predicted to increase notably (potentially >2×) in the high-stress samples.
hypothesis.baseline: The untreated, as-clad HEA with its inherent residual stresses and thermal expansion mismatch between phases.
hypothesis.boundary: The hypothesis applies under conditions of elevated temperature and cyclic thermal/mechanical loading where differential thermal expansion is pronounced; not applicable at room temperature or under static conditions.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Quantitative measures of the degradation amplification due to thermal expansion mismatches are difficult to precisely predict; the directional trend (increased degradation with higher stress) is robust but the exact factor is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one as-clad (with high residual thermal stresses) and one subjected to a subcritical annealing to relieve thermal stresses. Subject both to cyclic elevated temperature wear–corrosion tests and use non-destructive evaluation (e.g., acoustic emission, micro-CT) to monitor microcrack development along with standard wear and corrosion measurements.
measurements: Residual stress measurement via X-ray diffraction
Microcrack density using acoustic emission or micro-CT
Wear volume and corrosion current density measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the stress-relieved samples do not display a statistically lower microcrack density, wear rate, and corrosion rate compared to the as-clad samples under the same test conditions, the hypothesis that cyclic thermal expansion mismatch is driving the accelerated degradation is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: The Effect of Copper on the Microstructure, Wear and Corrosion Resistance of CoCrCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloys Manufactured by Powder Metallurgy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper demonstrated that phase segregation (with copper-rich FCC2 phase) and its spatial distribution strongly affect wear and corrosion (e.g., galvanic effects as seen in sections PMC9921093::web::018 and PMC9921093::web::010).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s findings by focusing on the role of mechanical microcracking at phase interfaces as the unifying mechanism of wear-corrosion synergy in multi-phase eutectic HEAs and proposes a controlled heat-treatment intervention to modify interfacial area.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Wear-induced microcracking at the phase boundaries accelerates degradation by exposing fresh metal and initiating localized galvanic corrosion between the hard, passivated matrix and the soft, copper-rich phase.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA with a fine-scale interpenetrating structure comprising a hard FCC matrix and a softer, copper-rich secondary phase having sharp interfaces.
hypothesis.intervention: Prepare two batches of the alloy: one processed normally and one with a heat treatment designed to coarsen the copper-rich phase (reducing the total interfacial area) without significantly altering bulk composition.
hypothesis.conditions: Elevated temperature under simultaneous wear (pin-on-disk type test) and exposure to a corrosive electrolyte (e.g., 3.5% NaCl) to mimic high-temperature wear-corrosion environments.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The integrity and distribution of the phase boundaries between the FCC matrix and the copper-rich phase.
hypothesis.mechanism: During wear at high temperature, the mechanical loading causes microcracking concentrated at the heterogeneous interfaces. These cracks repeatedly expose fresh metal to the electrolyte. The electrochemical potential difference between the hard, Cr-rich matrix and the copper-rich phase results in localized galvanic coupling, thereby accelerating anodic dissolution and oxide formation. The combined effect of mechanical disruption and galvanic corrosion leads to an increased overall degradation rate.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline with a fine, high-area interface, the heat-treated alloy having coarser, fewer interfaces should exhibit lower total degradation, with reduced corrosion rates on the softer phase and less pronounced wear–corrosion synergy. The baseline is expected to display approximately higher wear volume and increased corrosion current density relative to the coarsened variant.
hypothesis.baseline: Multi-phase eutectic HEA processed by standard powder metallurgy without deliberate heat treatment to alter phase coarseness.
hypothesis.boundary: Valid in the regime where the phases retain distinct electrochemical potentials and the interface microstructure is the dominant factor controlling crack initiation under wear (i.e., under conditions promoting micro-cracking and galvanic interaction).
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact quantitative differences between degradation rates depend on the extent of microcrack formation and the potential difference, which may vary with subtle compositional differences.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct wear-corrosion tests on two matched samples differing only in the copper-rich phase morphology (fine vs. coarsened). Monitor the evolution of microcracks via in situ microscopy and measure degradation via weight loss, corrosion current density, and wear track analysis.
measurements: Wear volume (mm³/N·m)
Corrosion current density (mA/cm²)
Microcrack density at phase boundaries (optical/SEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coarsened-phase sample does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in total degradation (wear and corrosion) and interfacial microcrack density compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: The Effect of Copper on the Microstructure, Wear and Corrosion Resistance of CoCrCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloys Manufactured by Powder Metallurgy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper noted that under tribological tests at elevated temperatures, oxide formation and subsequent delamination contribute to wear (PMC9921093::web::015), while literature on high-temperature corrosion highlights the role of passivation breakdown.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the concept of cyclic, tribologically induced oxide spallation due to thermal and mechanical mismatches as the single unified mechanism for accelerated degradation, and proposes an oxide-stabilization intervention to test it.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Cyclic spallation of oxide films induced by tribological loading and thermal mismatch leads to repeated passivation breakdown, driving accelerated degradation through simultaneous wear and corrosion.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA wherein different constituent phases form oxides of varying adherence and thermal expansion (e.g., a Cr-rich matrix forming protective Cr2O3 versus a copper-rich phase forming less protective Cu2O).
hypothesis.intervention: Apply an external stabilized, inert oxide coating (or post-oxidation treatment) on one set of samples to suppress cyclic oxide spallation, while leaving another set untreated.
hypothesis.conditions: Testing under high temperature and simultaneous mechanical sliding (wear) in a corrosive environment (e.g., chloride solution) where thermal cycling and frictional heating are significant.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The nature, adhesion, and thermal expansion mismatch of the oxide films on the different phases.
hypothesis.mechanism: At elevated temperature under mechanical wear, the oxide layers that form on the different phases (e.g., durable Cr2O3 on the matrix versus brittle Cu2O on the copper-rich phase) undergo cyclic spallation due to mismatches in thermal expansion and mechanical properties. This tribologically induced oxide removal repeatedly exposes the underlying metal to the harsh environment. The lack of stable, continuous passivation allows both wear and corrosion to proceed at an accelerated rate, as newly exposed surfaces are repeatedly subject to mechanical destruction and electrochemical attack.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the coated (or oxide-stabilized) sample should exhibit lower total degradation. Specifically, the untreated baseline will show higher wear rates (due to repeated oxide removal) and higher corrosion current density, leading to accelerated combined degradation. The magnitude of improvement is expected to be significant under conditions where thermal mismatch and spallation are pronounced.
hypothesis.baseline: Multi-phase eutectic HEA tested without any additional oxide stabilization treatment.
hypothesis.boundary: Mechanism is valid when the oxide film adhesion is poor and the thermal expansion mismatch is large, which is particularly relevant in alloys where distinct oxide types form on different phases.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Precise quantitative estimates of improvement depend on the coating stability and the frictional heating conditions; these parameters may vary with testing setup.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform comparative tribocorrosion tests at elevated temperature on two sets of samples: one with the pre-applied inert oxide coating and one with the natural oxide formation. Monitor the integrity of oxide films using in situ high-temperature microscopy and measure wear and corrosion performance via standard electrochemical and mechanical tests.
measurements: Wear volume (mm³/N·m)
Corrosion current density (mA/cm²)
Oxide film continuity and spallation frequency (via in situ imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the inert-coated samples do not show a statistically significant decrease in both wear and corrosion metrics compared to the untreated samples (or if oxide spallation rate remains unchanged), the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: High-Temperature Wear Behaviour of Spark Plasma Sintered AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The observed formation of heterogeneous oxide layers at high temperatures (PMC7515071::web::012) coupled with established principles of dopant-modified oxidation kinetics (TXT::wikipedia::Corrosion::014).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis directly connects element partitioning within the eutectic microstructure to non-uniform oxidation kinetics, leading to inhomogeneous oxide layers that accelerate coupled degradation, and proposes cerium doping as a targeted strategy to counteract this effect—a novel mechanistic link not proposed in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Non-uniform Oxidation Kinetics Driven by Element Partitioning Result in Inhomogeneous Oxide Scales That Promote Accelerated Coupled Degradation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An SPS-produced multiphase eutectic HEA where inherent segregation of alloying elements among phases leads to locally different oxidation kinetics and variable oxide compositions.
hypothesis.intervention: Dop the alloy with a small controlled amount of cerium, a reactive element known to promote uniform oxide growth and modify oxidation kinetics.
hypothesis.conditions: Reciprocating wear and corrosion tests at elevated temperature (900 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere with controlled mechanical cycling.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Regionally varying oxide scale compositions and thicknesses at phase boundaries arising from differential oxidation rates, resulting in weak spots that are prone to spallation under wear.
hypothesis.mechanism: Due to partitioning of major alloying elements during rapid solidification, different phases oxidize at different rates, leading to a non-uniform oxide layer in which some regions form thicker, more protective scales while others form thinner, less adherent films. The interfaces between these heterogeneous oxide regions become sites for crack initiation and accelerated material removal under mechanical wear. By introducing a minor cerium addition, the oxidation kinetics across the phases can be homogenized, as cerium segregates to oxide interfaces and promotes the formation of a more uniform, adherent, and slow-growing oxide layer. This reduces the frequency of oxide spallation and the ensuing exposure of fresh, reactive substrate, thereby lowering overall degradation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Cerium-doped samples should exhibit a more uniform oxide scale with fewer weak spots, leading to lower wear track depths and fewer corrosion pits relative to the baseline alloy. While both wear and corrosion rates are expected to be reduced, the precise quantification of improvement is subject to uncertainties in dopant distribution and its effects on oxidation kinetics.
hypothesis.baseline: Standard SPS-produced HEA exhibiting non-uniform oxidation due to intrinsic element partitioning, resulting in heterogeneous oxide scales at phase boundaries.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism becomes critical in regimes where oxidation kinetics vary significantly across phases; if the oxidation process is already highly uniform (e.g., due to different processing conditions), the effect of cerium doping might be minimal.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact improvement in oxide homogeneity and the corresponding reductions in wear and corrosion degradation rates are difficult to predict quantitatively and depend on the dopant’s distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from identical SPS batches: one with the standard composition and one doped with a minor amount of cerium. Conduct reciprocating wear tests at 900 °C. Post-test, characterize the oxide scale uniformity via cross-sectional SEM and XRD, measure wear track depth (LSM), and quantify corrosion pit density (SEM/EDS).
measurements: Oxide scale uniformity and phase composition (SEM, XRD)
Wear track depth (LSM)
Corrosion pit density (SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If cerium-doped samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in oxide scale uniformity, along with reduced wear track depths and lower corrosion pitting compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C8

source_paper.title: Refractory CrMoNbWV High-Entropy Alloy Manufactured by Mechanical Alloying and Spark Plasma Sintering: Evolution of Microstructure and Properties.

hypotheses.builds_on: This mechanism extends the paper’s observation that coarse oxide inclusions can act as crack initiation sites (PMC7866258::web::010) by proposing that service at elevated temperatures further drives oxide coarsening via grain boundary diffusion.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces the concept that post-sintering thermal management (e.g., rapid quenching) can control the oxide precipitate morphology, thereby influencing the coupled wear–corrosion degradation at elevated temperature—a parameter not previously investigated.

hypothesis.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, accelerated grain boundary diffusion promotes coarsening of pre-existing oxide precipitates, which weakens grain boundary cohesion and facilitates intergranular cracking that, when combined with sliding wear, exposes fresh metal that corrodes more rapidly.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multi-phase HEA with a BCC matrix, dispersed Laves phase precipitates, and fine oxide inclusions (such as NbVO4–VO) distributed along grain boundaries as formed after SPS.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a rapid quench immediately after sintering to 'freeze in' the fine dispersion of oxide precipitates, thereby preventing further coarsening during subsequent elevated-temperature service.
hypothesis.conditions: Wear–corrosion testing performed at elevated temperatures (300–400 °C) in a corrosive environment (e.g., 0.5 M acid) under sliding wear conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The size and distribution of oxide precipitates along grain boundaries, which govern grain boundary strength and the propensity to develop microcracks.
hypothesis.mechanism: When the alloy is exposed to elevated temperatures during wear–corrosion service, the enhanced grain boundary diffusion leads to the coarsening of oxide precipitates. Larger oxide inclusions become stress concentrators that reduce the cohesion of adjacent grain boundaries. Under mechanical sliding, these weakened sites initiate intergranular microcracks, exposing susceptible fresh metal surfaces to the corrosive environment. As corrosion accelerates at these cracked interfaces, the overall degradation (both wear and corrosion) increases substantially.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline with as-sintered oxide distribution that is allowed to coarsen during service, the quenched (fine oxide) samples should exhibit a lower density of intergranular cracks, reduced corrosion rates, and lower wear volume loss. The trend is qualitatively supported, though the precise improvement is uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: An HEA sample produced by standard SPS with no post-sintering rapid quench, thereby exhibiting coarser oxide precipitates after extended exposure to service temperatures.
hypothesis.boundary: Testing under elevated temperatures (300–400 °C) in a corrosive medium with sliding wear conditions that promote mechanical stress at grain boundaries.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative difference in degradation resulting from finer versus coarser oxide precipitate distributions is uncertain due to the complex interplay between diffusion kinetics and mechanical stress.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA specimens: one group receives a rapid quench post-SPS to obtain a fine, uniform oxide dispersion, while the other follows the standard cooling route and develops coarser oxide precipitates. Subject both groups to identical elevated-temperature wear–corrosion tests. Post-test, evaluate grain boundary crack density, corrosion performance (via icorr), and wear loss.
measurements: Grain boundary oxide size/distribution (via SEM/TEM)
Crack density characterization (microscopy)
Electrochemical corrosion current density (icorr)
Wear track volume loss
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the quenched, fine-oxide samples do not exhibit significantly lower crack density, corrosion current, and wear loss compared to the standard-cooled samples, then the hypothesis that oxide precipitate coarsening drives accelerated degradation is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that a stable, dense glaze layer in NiX reduces wear at high temperatures, now extended to consider conditions where the glaze is mechanically compromised.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically integrates mechanical disruption of the protective oxide (glaze) layer into the degradation mechanism under simultaneous wear and corrosion—a dynamic interplay not addressed in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation arises because mechanical wear under high-temperature corrosive conditions disrupts the formation and integrity of a protective glaze layer, leading to enhanced oxidation and subsequent material loss.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA that, under high-temperature sliding, is capable of forming a protective glaze layer (oxide film) that usually mitigates wear when intact.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the test environment to include an additional abrasive component (or increased sliding speed/force) that is known to disrupt oxide layer formation, then compare with a scenario where the glaze layer is allowed to form undisturbed.
hypothesis.conditions: Elevated temperature (600–800 °C) in an oxidizing, corrosive atmosphere during sliding wear where tribo-oxidation can occur but is challenged by mechanical removal.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A glaze layer formed by tribo-oxidation that normally acts as a protective barrier at the sliding interface.
hypothesis.mechanism: Under typical conditions, tribo-oxidation generates a dense, protective oxide glaze that reduces direct metal-to-environment contact and minimizes wear. However, under simultaneous high-wear conditions, mechanical abrasion intermittently erodes this glaze, exposing vulnerable substrate areas to rapid oxidation. The recurring cycle of glaze disruption and reformation leads to an overall thinner, less protective oxide film and consequently higher rates of both oxidation (corrosion) and wear.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy where the glaze layer remains intact, the disrupted-glaze condition should yield an increase in overall degradation by about 50–100% (with increased wear track depth and higher oxygen uptake) due to enhanced oxidation and accelerated wear.
hypothesis.baseline: A controlled scenario wherein the sliding conditions are moderated (reduced load or sliding speed) to allow continuous formation and stability of the natural glaze layer.
hypothesis.boundary: The hypothesis applies when the environmental oxygen is sufficiently high to support glaze formation but also under conditions where mechanical stresses exceed the glaze’s adhesion strength; if wear energy is too low, the glaze remains intact.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact quantitative effects of glaze disruption are challenging to predict without detailed experimental data on glaze adhesion energies and abrasion rates.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform sliding wear tests at high temperatures on two sets of specimens: one under conditions promoting stable glaze formation (lower load/speed) and one under conditions known to disrupt the glaze (higher load/speed or with abrasive additives). Use surface analysis (SEM, XPS) to assess oxide layer continuity.
measurements: Glaze layer integrity (thickness, continuity) via cross-sectional microscopy
Wear volume
Oxygen content on the worn surfaces via EDS/XPS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the disruption-prone condition does not show significantly lower glaze layer coverage and the degradation rates do not increase compared to the control, then the hypothesis that glaze disruption is causing accelerated degradation is refuted.

hypotheses.label: C11

source_paper.title: High-Temperature Wear Properties of Laser Powder Directed Energy Deposited Ferritic Stainless Steel 430.

hypotheses.builds_on: The positive correlation between hardness and wear resistance found in LP-DED FSS430 (as reported in PMC12299124) is extended to hypothesize that hardness differentials in a eutectic HEA drive synergistic galvanic corrosion.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the concept that micro-galvanic effects from differential phase wear—in addition to mechanical wear—are the root cause of accelerated degradation in a eutectic HEA, and it proposes a microalloying strategy to counteract this mechanism.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Accelerated degradation is driven by differential phase wear in the eutectic HEA: A softer phase preferentially wears away, leaving harder phases protruding and setting up localized galvanic couples. The resulting potential differences at phase interfaces exacerbate both localized corrosion and mechanical removal.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic HEA with phases exhibiting different hardness and electrical potentials, leading to an intrinsic micro-galvanic system.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce minor microalloying additions (e.g., boron) to homogenize the hardness and alter the electrochemical behavior at phase boundaries, thereby reducing galvanic potential differences.
hypothesis.conditions: Simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosive environments at elevated temperature (e.g., 500 °C), where differences in phase hardness and stability are pronounced.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: More uniform distribution of hardness and reduced potential gradients at phase boundaries due to altered grain boundary chemistry.
hypothesis.mechanism: In the untreated alloy, uneven wear causes softer phase removal and exposes harder, nobler phases that become anodic relative to their surroundings. This galvanic mismatch accelerates corrosion locally, and the resulting degradation further enhances wear. The boron addition is expected to refine and equalize microstructural hardness, reducing galvanic coupling and hence the synergy between wear and corrosion.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the boron-modified alloy should exhibit a lower overall degradation rate with decreased wear volume and mitigated corrosion at the phase interfaces (direction: improvement; precise reduction magnitude remains uncertain).
hypothesis.baseline: Eutectic HEA without boron addition, where constituent phases differ significantly in mechanical and electrochemical properties.
hypothesis.boundary: Samples evaluated under the same elevated temperature (≈500 °C) and corrosive-cum-wear conditions with controlled sliding contact.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the directional improvements are supported by analogous behavior in Ni3Al alloys, the precise quantitative difference is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of the HEA: one with a minor boron addition and one without. Subject both to high-temperature sliding wear in a corrosive environment. Measure local potentials at interfaces and quantify wear and corrosion damage.
measurements: Local electrochemical potential mapping
Wear volume measurement
Corrosion attack depth and mass loss analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-added samples do not show a significant reduction in localized galvanic corrosion and related wear compared to the baseline, or if potential differences remain comparable, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes that not only the presence but the size and distribution of TiB2 particles are critical at elevated temperatures; coarse TiB2 agglomerates act as focal points for passive film failure, a mechanistic detail not addressed in the original work.

hypothesis.hypothesis: TiB2 Agglomeration‐Induced Passive Film Disruption Accelerates Coupled Degradation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA produced by laser cladding in which in situ formed TiB2 particles exist in a range of morphologies from well‐dispersed fine particles to locally agglomerated/coarse clusters.
hypothesis.intervention: Control and intentionally modify processing parameters (e.g., slight increases in boron content or adjustment of laser parameters) that promote TiB2 agglomeration, thereby altering their dispersion within the dendritic (DR) region.
hypothesis.conditions: Exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (e.g., >300°C) where oxidation kinetics and mechanical abrasion are both activated.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The morphology and spatial distribution of TiB2 reinforcements and the resulting continuity or disruption of the passive oxide film along phase boundaries.
hypothesis.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the TiB2 coarse agglomerates create local stress concentrations and surface irregularities that disrupt the formation and adherence of the protective oxide film. hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy with a well‐dispersed, fine TiB2 distribution, the alloy engineered to have more agglomerated/coarse TiB2 is expected to exhibit higher wear rates and increased corrosion current densities—resulting in a higher total degradation rate. hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is significant only when the operating temperature sufficiently accelerates oxidation kinetics and the wear conditions mechanically stress the heterogeneous oxide film; under milder conditions the effect may be negligible.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of TiB2 agglomeration on degradation rates requires investigation, and the trade-off between particle size and beneficial reinforcement (at lower temperatures) versus detrimental effects (at elevated temperatures) remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic HEA samples via laser cladding that differ primarily in the distribution of TiB2: one with a controlled fine dispersion and one with intentionally agglomerated/coarse TiB2 (achieved via slight processing changes or higher boron levels). Subject both sets to identical high-temperature wear–corrosion tests (e.g., 350°C in a corrosive medium under steady sliding wear).

Wear rate and damage assessment (wear track profiling).
Electrochemical corrosion tests (icorr, Rct, EIS measurements) with mapping of passive film integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with agglomerated TiB2 do not show statistically significant higher wear rates, lower passive film resistance, and increased corrosion current density than the finely dispersed control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: Investigation of surface hardness, thermostability, tribo-corrosion, and microstructural morphological properties of microwave-synthesized high entropy alloy FeCoNiMnCu coating claddings on steel.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a post-processing annealing step to optimize the microstructural and residual stress state of the HEA cladding, thereby enhancing the stability of the protective oxide scale—a strategy not applied in the original study.

hypothesis.material_initial_state: An as-cladded high-entropy alloy featuring a heterogeneous microstructure with inherent residual stresses and locally disrupted oxide layers, as evidenced by observed cracks at the cladding interface.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement a controlled post-cladding annealing treatment (for example, heating the samples to 850 °C for 1 hour in air followed by controlled cooling) prior to service exposure.
hypothesis.conditions: Service conditions at elevated temperature (~800 °C) under simultaneous wear (e.g., pin-on-disc testing) and corrosive attack (immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A more homogeneous microstructure with reduced residual stresses that promotes the formation of a uniform, adherent, and continuous oxide scale on the HEA surface.
hypothesis.mechanism: In the baseline state, compositional variations and residual stresses in the as-cladded HEA promote the development of a patchy oxide scale that is easily spalled during wear, leading to accelerated corrosion.
