hypothesis.baseline: The original as-cladded high-entropy alloy without subsequent annealing treatment.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect hinges on annealing conditions that avoid detrimental phase coarsening; if over-annealing occurs, improvement might be negated.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The trade-off between residual stress relief and potential phase coarsening during annealing introduces uncertainty in the net improvement magnitude.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples from the same cladded HEA batch: one set remains as-cladded, and the other undergoes the specified annealing treatment. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature wear-corrosion tests (800 °C with 3.5 wt% NaCl and controlled cyclic wear). Assess the microstructure and oxide layer (via SEM and XRD stress measurements) and compare mass loss and corrosion pit metrics.
measurements: Microstructural uniformity and grain size analysis via SEM.
Residual stress evaluation using XRD stress measurements.
Mass loss and wear track depth measurements after testing.
Corrosion pit density and depth via surface imaging.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements (i.e., lower residual stress, more uniform oxide scale, reduced wear and corrosion damage) compared to as-cladded samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C7

source_paper.title: Refractory CrMoNbWV High-Entropy Alloy Manufactured by Mechanical Alloying and Spark Plasma Sintering: Evolution of Microstructure and Properties.

hypotheses.builds_on: This hypothesis builds on observations in the paper of a carburized layer (PMC7866258::web::010) and its reported influence on wear and corrosion, extending the mechanism to elevated-temperature conditions where carbon diffusion is further enhanced.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It explicitly proposes that excessive carburization at elevated temperatures produces localized carbide precipitation at phase boundaries, promoting interfacial embrittlement that couples wear and corrosion—a mechanism not addressed in the original study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Elevated-temperature carburization accelerates coupled degradation by inducing interfacial embrittlement via carbon uptake and carbide precipitation along phase boundaries.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multi-phase high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a BCC solid-solution matrix, dispersed Laves phase precipitates, and a carburized surface layer (as observed after SPS using graphite dies).
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce an inert barrier/coating on the inner walls of the sintering die (or use an alternative die material) to suppress carbon diffusion during SPS, thereby reducing carburization.
hypothesis.conditions: Wear–corrosion tests at elevated temperatures (e.g., 300–400 °C) in a corrosive medium (such as 0.5 M H2SO4 or a chloride solution) under controlled sliding wear conditions similar to ASTM G65.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Carbon diffusion–induced lattice strains and the formation of fine, brittle carbide particles specifically localizing at interfaces between the ductile BCC matrix and harder Laves phase precipitates.
hypothesis.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, enhanced carbon diffusion from the graphite die causes carbon intercalation into the BCC lattice, promoting the precipitation of fine HEA carbides at or near phase boundaries. This locally increases lattice strain and embrittles the interphase region, leading to interface debonding under mechanical sliding. Exposure of the freshly fractured metal in these regions then results in accelerated local corrosion, thereby coupling wear and corrosion into a markedly higher total degradation rate.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline sample with standard carburization, the sample made with an inert die (showing reduced carbon uptake) should exhibit lower total degradation. In particular, one would expect a decrease in the wear volume loss and lower corrosion current density. The direction of change is supported qualitatively, while the exact magnitude of improvement is uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: An as-sintered HEA sample produced in a standard graphite die (allowing typical carburization), tested under identical elevated-temperature wear–corrosion conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: Testing must occur at temperatures high enough (e.g., 300–400 °C) to accentuate carbon diffusion kinetics and be performed under a corrosive environment (acidic or chloride-based) coupled with mechanical sliding stresses.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The quantitative impact of reduced carbon uptake on long-term degradation rates is uncertain because complex interactions between carbide precipitate morphology and oxide passivation may also play a role.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA samples: one set produced in a standard graphite die (allowing normal carburization) and another set produced with an inert-coated die to minimize carbon uptake. Subject both groups to identical simultaneous wear–corrosion tests at elevated temperature (300–400 °C) in a corrosive medium. Assess wear volume loss and corrosion current density for each group.
measurements: Carbon content and carbide phase distribution (via EDS/TEM)
Wear track volume loss
Corrosion current density (via electrochemical Tafel analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the inert-die samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in both the wear loss and corrosion rate compared to the standard samples, then the hypothesis that carbon-induced interfacial embrittlement drives the accelerated degradation is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C15

source_paper.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.

hypotheses.builds_on: the understanding from the paper that different microstructural regions play distinct roles in wear and corrosion, combined with general principles of high-temperature oxidation and galvanic coupling from corrosion science.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely integrates the effect of differential oxide growth at inherent microstructural interfaces (dendritic vs interdendritic) and shows how their interaction under elevated temperatures accelerates degradation through localized galvanic effects—a mechanistic detail not previously considered in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Differential Oxide Growth at Dendritic–Interdendritic Interfaces Accelerates Degradation via Enhanced Galvanic Coupling.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic HEA with distinct dendritic (DR) and interdendritic (IR) regions that naturally form different passive oxide layers due to compositional variations.
hypothesis.intervention: Leverage the intrinsic differences by operating under elevated temperature conditions to promote differential oxide growth; no compositional modification is introduced but the condition (temperature) is tuned to exaggerate oxide layer heterogeneity.
hypothesis.conditions: Simultaneous exposure to wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures (>300°C) where oxidation is accelerated and mechanical wear can selectively remove less-protective oxide regions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The heterogeneous passive films formed at the DR–IR interfaces, where the differences in oxide composition and thickness create localized sites of weakness.
hypothesis.mechanism: Elevated temperature accelerates oxidation and promotes the formation of passive films that differ in composition and adhesion on the dendritic versus interdendritic areas. Mechanical wear then preferentially removes the thinner or less adherent oxide in one region, exposing underlying phases with differing electrochemical potentials. This leads to strong galvanic coupling at the phase boundaries where the oxide is disrupted, thereby locally accelerating corrosion that feeds back into increased wear. The synergy between nonuniform oxide formation and selective film removal under wear conditions leads to accelerated coupled degradation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline tested at a lower temperature (with more uniform oxide films), the HEA under elevated temperature is expected to show a significant increase in total degradation. Specifically, higher corrosion current density and increased wear damage (deeper and wider wear tracks) are predicted, though the precise magnitude depends on the degree of oxide heterogeneity.
hypothesis.baseline: The same eutectic HEA operating under conditions where the oxide film forms more uniformly (e.g., lower temperature or under static conditions), resulting in a more homogeneous passive layer that better resists wear-corrosion coupling.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant when temperature is high enough to drive significantly different oxidation kinetics in the two regions and when wear stress can externally remove the weaker oxide portions; under isothermal or low-stress conditions the effect may be reduced.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact relative contributions of differential oxide formation and mechanical wear in driving galvanic coupling are not yet well quantified, making precise predictions of degradation rates uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the multi-phase eutectic HEA and expose them to high-temperature (e.g., 350°C) simultaneous wear–corrosion tests versus a matched set at a lower temperature. Use surface imaging (SEM/EDS) to map oxide film uniformity across dendritic vs interdendritic regions and conduct localized electrochemical measurements along with wear track profilometry.
measurements: Mapping of oxide film thickness and composition across DR and IR regions.
Electrochemical tests (icorr, EIS) taken from micro-regions.
Wear track characterization (depth and morphology).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If elevated temperature does not induce significant oxide layer heterogeneity at the DR–IR interfaces, or if the increased heterogeneity does not correlate with a measurable increase in galvanic corrosion and wear damage compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

expert_context.question: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

hypotheses.label: C2

source_paper.title: Investigation of surface hardness, thermostability, tribo-corrosion, and microstructural morphological properties of microwave-synthesized high entropy alloy FeCoNiMnCu coating claddings on steel.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s findings on protective oxide formation (Cr2O3 and spinel phases) and principles from thermal barrier coatings that emphasize the role of graded interfaces, extending them by intentionally modifying composition to promote a beneficial amorphous alumina phase.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a compositional modification (minor Al addition) that leverages in situ oxidation during tribo-corrosion to form a graded, protective interlayer—an approach distinct from simply relying on the oxide layers formed during high-temperature exposure in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor Al addition into the HEA promotes in situ formation of an amorphous alumina-rich interlayer during tribo-corrosion, which stabilizes a graded, mechanically robust and electrochemically inert interface that governs degradation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A microwave-cladded FeCoNiMnCu high-entropy alloy coating on SS-304 with uniform equiatomic composition and an oxide layer formed during thermal exposure.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the cladding powder composition by substituting a small fraction (~5 wt%) of one of the base elements with Al, creating an Al-doped HEA. This minor change is designed to enable in situ formation of amorphous Al2O3 during tribo-corrosion testing.
hypothesis.conditions: Conduct parallel tribo-corrosion tests under identical conditions (pin-on-disc testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl) for the Al-doped HEA and the baseline FeCoNiMnCu HEA. Ensure that testing conditions provide sufficient exposure to oxygen so that oxidation reactions can proceed during wear.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A graded interlayer at the worn surface comprising amorphous Al2O3 mixed with high-entropy oxide phases, which acts as a barrier to both mechanical wear and electrochemical degradation.
hypothesis.mechanism: The minor Al addition facilitates localized oxidation under tribological stress to form amorphous alumina, which blends with existing oxide phases to produce a graded, mechanically continuous and chemically inert barrier. This interlayer reduces galvanic interaction and limits ion transport, thus lowering both wear and corrosion rates.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped HEA is expected to show improved tribo-corrosion resistance compared to the baseline HEA, with reduced wear depth and lower corrosion currents. The enhancement might be in the order of a 20–40% reduction in degradation metrics, though precise values are uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: Untreated, equiatomic FeCoNiMnCu HEA coatings without any Al addition.
hypothesis.boundary: This prediction should hold under conditions where oxygen is available for in situ oxidation and where the minor Al addition does not disrupt the overall mechanical integrity of the HEA; it may fail in highly oxygen-deprived environments or if the Al content exceeds the optimal threshold, leading to embrittlement.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal amount of Al addition and the exact structure and continuity of the graded oxide interlayer under real tribo-corrosion conditions require further characterization, and quantitative improvements are approximate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of HEA coatings with a 5 wt% Al addition and one set with the baseline FeCoNiMnCu composition. Subject both sets to identical tribo-corrosion (pin-on-disc in NaCl) tests and perform surface characterization (SEM, TEM, XRD) to detect the presence and structure of the graded oxide interlayer. Correlate wear rates and electrochemical corrosion parameters between the two groups.
measurements: Wear rate (mass loss and wear track analysis)
Corrosion rate (potentiodynamic polarization, EIS)
Surface oxide composition and layer structure (XRD, TEM, XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped samples do not exhibit an amorphous, graded oxide interlayer and do not show statistically significant improvements in both wear and corrosion resistance relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis that the Al-induced graded barrier controls the coupled response is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C12

source_paper.title: Titanium-induced phase changes and tribological behavior in cantor-based high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper documents that Ti addition drives phase transformation and multiphase formation in HEAs. This hypothesis extends that observation by linking the inherent multiphase microstructure to micro-galvanic corrosion under sliding conditions, and proposes a homogenization treatment to mitigate this effect.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely proposes that adjusting the micro-galvanic interactions through post-processing homogenization—not just altering the composition—can serve as the single governing mechanism to control the coupled wear and corrosion behavior in HEAs under tribocorrosion.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The micro-galvanic coupling between dissimilar phases within the multiphase HEA governs the tribocorrosion response; by reducing the electrochemical potential differences among FCC, BCC, and intermetallic regions via a homogenization anneal, the synergistic degradation from wear-enhanced localized corrosion can be minimized.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A cantorial HEA with a heterogeneous multiphase microstructure (containing distinct regions of FCC matrix, BCC, and Laves intermetallic phases formed through mechanical alloying and SPS) that inherently exhibits potential differences between the phases.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a post-SPS homogenization anneal (at an optimized temperature and time) designed to reduce compositional and structural segregation between phases, thereby lowering the electrochemical potential differences among them.
hypothesis.conditions: Perform comparative tribocorrosion tests using a pin-on-disc assay in a chloride-containing solution (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) at ambient temperature on homogenized (annealed) samples versus conventionally processed (non-annealed) ones under identical testing parameters.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A more chemically and structurally homogenized near-surface microstructure with reduced phase boundary contrasts, leading to diminished localized galvanic cells.
hypothesis.mechanism: In the multiphase HEA, dissimilar phases with different electrochemical potentials form micro-galvanic couples that accelerate localized corrosion when exposed to a corrosive medium especially under dynamic wear conditions. A controlled homogenization anneal reduces the segregation of alloying elements between phases, thereby minimizing potential gradients. With lower micro-galvanic driving forces, the rate of localized corrosion during sliding is reduced. Although mechanical wear remains similar, the overall tribocorrosion degradation decreases owing to suppressed corrosion activity.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The homogenized HEA is expected to exhibit a lower corrosion current density (and thus lower total degradation due to tribocorrosion) compared to the as-sintered, heterogeneous material. The wear rate might be similar or only slightly increased, but the reduced corrosion should yield an overall improvement in service life.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-sintered, un-annealed HEA coating with a clearly segmented multiphase microstructure that leads to significant micro-galvanic interactions under tribological stress.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is effective when the homogenization anneal can sufficiently reduce potential differences without overly coarsening the microstructure. It may fail if the anneal promotes grain growth or unwanted phase transformations that negate the benefits of reduced galvanic coupling.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal annealing parameters that balance homogenization with retention of desired mechanical properties remain uncertain, and the extent to which micro-galvanic coupling contributes quantitatively to tribocorrosion in these alloys is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one that undergoes a controlled homogenization anneal post-SPS, and a control that remains in the as-sintered state. Subject both sets to identical tribocorrosion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl. Use local electrochemical techniques (such as scanning Kelvin probe force microscopy or microelectrochemical cells) to map potential differences at phase boundaries, and measure overall wear, corrosion rates, and surface morphology before and after testing.
measurements: Local electrochemical potential mapping at phase boundaries
Wear rate (mm³/N·m)
Corrosion current density and impedance measurements
Microstructural and compositional homogeneity (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the homogenized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in local potential differences and corresponding improvement in corrosion resistance (with overall tribocorrosion degradation comparable to or worse than the control), the hypothesis will be falsified.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding from the paper that fine TiB2 formation (at x = 0.5) improves wear and corrosion by refining microstructure and aiding passive film stability.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s results by coupling the microstructural aspect (grain and particle dispersion) with the mechanism of passive film self-healing during simultaneous wear and corrosion, proposing that controlled particle size/distribution is critical for the synergistic tribo-corrosion resistance.

hypothesis.hypothesis: In a tribo-corrosion environment, the coupling between wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is governed by the stability and self-healing of the passive film, which is enhanced by the presence of finely dispersed in situ TiB2 particles. These particles act as nucleation sites for passive film repair and mitigate localized galvanic cells by reducing cathodic area differences during mechanical wear.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A base AlCoCrFeNiMoTi high-entropy alloy prepared via laser cladding, initially featuring a dual-phase BCC + σ structure without excessive coarse ceramic particles.
hypothesis.intervention: Control the boron addition and laser cladding parameters to produce a uniform dispersion of fine TiB2 reinforcements rather than clustered or oversized particles.
hypothesis.conditions: Experiments conducted in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution under sliding wear conditions (20 N load, similar to the original study parameters) to simulate tribo-corrosion.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed fine TiB2 particles distributed within the alloy matrix and at phase boundaries.
hypothesis.mechanism: The fine TiB2 particles promote grain refinement and provide active sites for rapid passive film regeneration when the film is mechanically disrupted by wear. They also reduce galvanic coupling by limiting the size and continuity of cathodic sites (e.g., large TiB2 clusters), thereby simultaneously reducing the wear rate and the corrosion current density.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline with either no or excessive boron addition, the optimized dispersion is expected to reduce the total degradation by lowering wear rate (potentially by ~50% relative improvement over a coarse-particle sample) and decreasing corrosion current density (icorr reduction similar to or improved upon the 51% reduction seen with small boron addition).
hypothesis.baseline: The baseline is the same HEA coating without controlled fine TiB2 distribution (either B-free or with coarse/agglomerated TiB2 particles).
hypothesis.boundary: The prediction should hold in environments where mechanical wear intermittently disrupts the passive film, such as in mild to moderate tribo-corrosion conditions. It may fail if the tribological load is so high that even rapid film regeneration cannot compensate for film removal, or if the environmental corrosivity overwhelms the passive film healing.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in wear and corrosion metrics is uncertain beyond qualitative trends, and scale-up effects during extended cycling are not quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one with controlled fine TiB2 dispersion (via optimized boron content and laser parameters) and one with either no boron or with excessive boron leading to coarse TiB2. Subject both to identical tribo-corrosion tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl under sliding wear conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (via Archard’s law)
Corrosion current density (icorr) from potentiodynamic polarization
Passive film quality (thickness and continuity via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized coating does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in both reduced wear rate and lower corrosion current density relative to the baseline, or if passive film continuity is not improved, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: Enhanced Wear and Corrosion Resistance of AlCoCrFeNiMoTi High-Entropy Alloy via B Addition by Laser Cladding.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s demonstration that an optimal amount of boron improves the distribution of TiB2 and thereby enhances both wear resistance and corrosion performance.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a dual role for the microstructure by emphasizing not only the mechanical hardening effect of TiB2 but also its contribution to passive film integrity through effective stress distribution and debris trapping, an integrated mechanism not explicitly explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by the synergistic interaction between ductile matrix deformation and the dispersion of reinforcing ceramic phases (TiB2), which together determine the integrity of the passive film. In a well-balanced microstructure, embedded fine TiB2 particles help distribute local stress and trap wear debris, thus prolonging passive film continuity and mitigating localized galvanic corrosion.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy system (AlCoCrFeNiMoTi) produced via laser cladding, with an initial dual-phase (BCC + σ) microstructure that already contains in situ formed TiB2 particles but with variable distribution and particle sizes.
hypothesis.intervention: Adjust both compositional parameters (subtle boron variation) and processing conditions to achieve a tailored microstructure featuring a bimodal distribution: a ductile continuous matrix with uniformly dispersed, submicron TiB2 particles, avoiding excessive agglomeration.
hypothesis.conditions: Perform tribo-corrosion tests combining sliding wear (under controlled load and speed) and electrochemical corrosion testing in corrosive media (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl) to assess interactive effects.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The optimized interface between the ductile matrix and well-dispersed fine TiB2 particles, which act jointly to maintain a stable, self-healing passive film.
hypothesis.mechanism: The ductile matrix accommodates mechanical deformation and absorbs wear impacts while the embedded fine TiB2 particles serve as micro-scale reinforcements that arrest crack propagation and capture wear debris, preventing them from acting as galvanic sites. This synergy maintains passive film integrity by both physically reinforcing the surface and reducing local stress concentrations that can initiate film breakdown, resulting in coupled improvements in wear resistance and corrosion protection.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline with either a purely ductile microstructure or one with coarse, agglomerated TiB2 particles, the optimized bimodal microstructure is predicted to show lower wear rates and extended passive film life (lower corrosion current and delayed pitting initiation). The overall degradation should visibly decline, although exact quantitative improvements are uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: HEA coatings produced with either no adjustment or with excessive boron that leads to coarse TiB2 agglomerates.
hypothesis.boundary: The hypothesis holds in environments where both mechanical stress and corrosive attack occur concurrently and the matrix-ceramic interface remains stable. It may not hold if the mechanical loads cause catastrophic matrix failure or if the ceramic particles are dislodged extensively, which could then generate new active corrosion sites.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The relative contributions of matrix ductility versus ceramic reinforcement in passive film maintenance are not precisely quantifiable, making the magnitude of synergy somewhat uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two comparison groups: one with the optimized bimodal microstructure (fine, uniformly dispersed TiB2 in a ductile matrix) and another with either a soft, unreinforced matrix or one with excessive, coarse TiB2 deposits. Subject both groups to identical tribo-corrosion testing regimes and monitor the evolution of passive film characteristics and degradation rates.
measurements: Wear rate and spallation characteristics
Electrochemical measurements (potentiodynamic polarization for icorr and pitting potential)
Surface and cross-sectional imaging to assess passive film integrity and wear debris distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized microstructure does not achieve significantly better wear-corrosion resistance (improved passive film durability and lower degradation metrics) compared to the baseline samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C3

source_paper.title: Study on cavitation erosion-corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high entropy alloy in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation that CE boosts oxygen transport and intermittently damages the passive film (PMC11378927::web::015) and the interplay between passive film growth/disruption cycles seen in the OCP curves.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a targeted heat-treatment strategy to stabilize the passive film, directly testing whether enhanced re-passivation kinetics can mitigate the synergistic tribo-corrosion effect—an approach not reported in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The tribo-corrosion response of the HEA is governed by the dynamic stability of its passive oxide film, where mechanical wear intermittently disrupts the protective film and the re-passivation kinetics dictate the coupled degradation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA with its inherent multiphase microstructure and naturally formed passive film in corrosive environments.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a controlled post-casting heat treatment aimed at optimizing the oxide scale formation (e.g., a short-term oxidation heat treatment in air) to generate a more uniform and adherent passive film.
hypothesis.conditions: Testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl under cyclic tribological loading (mimicking tribo-corrosion conditions) in a controlled laboratory setup.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A modified and more chemically bonded oxide film covering a more homogenized microstructure.
hypothesis.mechanism: Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the mechanical removal of the passive film exposes fresh material; if the re-passivation kinetics are slow, the corrosion component is enhanced due to localized attack (as observed by potential shifts and EN analysis in the paper). Enhancing film formation via heat treatment should lead to a resilient passive layer that is less prone to mechanical disruption, thereby reducing the cycle of damage and repassivation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The heat-treated HEA will show lower total mass loss compared to the untreated baseline, with a decrease in corrosion-driven degradation while the wear component might be similar. The improved re-passivation should result in a measurable reduction in corrosion current (Icorr) and more stable open-circuit potential curves under cyclic loading.
hypothesis.baseline: The original as-cast, untreated CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA under identical tribo-corrosion testing conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: The prediction holds if the failure mode is mostly driven by passive film disruption rather than by bulk mechanical damage. It might fail in regimes where excessive mechanical loading completely removes the oxide regardless of its adhesion.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise degree of improvement in re-passivation kinetics and its quantitative effect on mass loss under tribo-corrosion is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples; one set subject to the optimized oxidation heat treatment and one set left as-cast. Expose both sets to identical cyclic tribo-corrosion tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl while monitoring mass loss, electrochemical parameters (OCP, Icorr), and surface film integrity via SEM/EDS.
measurements: Cumulative mass loss over time
Potentiodynamic polarization curves
Surface film morphology and composition
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate (Icorr) and total degradation compared to the as-cast control, or if the improved film does not persist under mechanical action, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C7

source_paper.title: Effect of Thermal Shock on Properties of a Strongly Amorphous AlCrTiZrMo High-Entropy Alloy Film.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s finding that a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide can effectively protect against oxidation, extended by considering how thermal processing (cooling rates) can tune the residual stress and microstructural gradation of the oxide, thereby governing tribo-corrosion behavior.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the idea that post-annealing cooling rate can be deliberately modified to create a graded oxide layer with improved mechanical integrity and corrosion resistance—a processing parameter not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Post-annealing cooling rate controls the formation of a graded, low‐stress oxide scale that governs the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An amorphous AlCrTiZrMo HEA film deposited by Co-FCVAD that, when annealed at 800 °C for 1 h, forms a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer.
hypothesis.intervention: After high-temperature annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, apply two different controlled cooling protocols: one with slow, furnace cooling and one with rapid quenching.
hypothesis.conditions: Both sets of samples are subjected to the same tribo-corrosion testing in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution using a reciprocating sliding setup.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A graded oxide scale featuring a gradual transition in microstructure and residual stress from the outer, hard ZrTiO4 layer to the underlying HEA substrate.
hypothesis.mechanism: Slow cooling minimizes thermal gradients and residual tensile stresses in the oxide, allowing the formation of a coherent graded oxide layer with fewer microcracks. This graded structure enhances both wear and corrosion resistance by reducing crack initiation (mechanically) and hindering oxygen diffusion (electrochemically). In contrast, rapid quenching can introduce high residual stresses and microcrack networks within the oxide, which would accelerate degradation under tribological and corrosive loading. (See also TXT::wikipedia::Thermal_barrier_coating::004 for the importance of matching thermal stresses.)
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples will exhibit lower overall degradation, with reduced wear rates and smaller fluctuations in OCP (ΔOCP) compared to quenched samples. The improvement is expected to be moderate—likely on the order of 15–30% lower degradation markers—if thermal shock does not override the graded oxide benefits.
hypothesis.baseline: The standard processing route with rapid cooling (or uncontrolled cooling) immediately after annealing at 800 °C.
hypothesis.boundary: This effect should hold in environments where thermal gradients during cooling can be controlled. In service conditions that impose very rapid cyclic thermal shocks or where cooling rates are dictated by external conditions, the benefits might be diminished.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement depends on the cooling rate achieved and the stress relaxation kinetics; detailed thermal analysis is required to optimize parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical HEA films annealed at 800 °C for 1 h. One set is slowly furnace-cooled (e.g., cooling at 1-2 °C/min) while the other is quenched in room-temperature air or inert medium. Subject both sets to identical reciprocating tribo-corrosion tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution and measure wear rates, OCP fluctuations, and oxide microstructure (using SEM and XRD stress analysis).
measurements: Wear rate (mm³·N⁻¹·m⁻¹)
ΔOCP during the wear cycle
Residual stress/microcrack density in the oxide (via SEM/XRD)
Oxide layer thickness and gradation (via cross-sectional analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slow-cooled samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and ΔOCP and do not show evidence of a graded, lower-stress oxide microstructure compared to the quenched samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C8

source_paper.title: Effect of Heat Treatment Duration on the Recrystallization and Electrochemical Properties of Cold-Rolled Cantor-Type High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s findings on the role of residual stress reduction in improving corrosion resistance, extending that concept by actively inducing beneficial compressive stresses through a mechanical surface treatment
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces laser shock peening as a novel surface engineering approach to simultaneously control wear and corrosion in HEAs under tribo-corrosion conditions, a strategy not previously explored in the discussed paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The coupled tribo‐corrosion performance is governed by the near-surface residual stress state, where introducing compressive residual stresses can retard wear-induced crack and passive film failure and thus mitigate both mechanical and corrosive degradation.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A conventional high-entropy Cantor alloy produced by cold rolling and subsequent heat treatment that results in relatively low residual compressive stress at the surface.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply laser shock peening (LSP) to the heat-treated HEA surfaces to induce deep and sustained compressive residual stresses and refine the near-surface grain structure.
hypothesis.conditions: Conduct tribo-corrosion experiments involving sliding wear in a corrosive environment (3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) with controlled mechanical loading and temperature.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The enhanced compressive residual stress field and a refined near-surface microstructure that together improve the adhesion and resilience of the protective Cr2O3 passive film.
hypothesis.mechanism: The induced compressive stresses from LSP inhibit crack initiation and growth when the passive film is mechanically disturbed by wear. The resulting refined surface microstructure further promotes rapid repassivation, reducing the susceptibility of grain boundaries to anodic dissolution under tribological stress.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a non-peened baseline, specimens subjected to LSP should exhibit lower wear mass loss and a reduced corrosion rate, evidenced by lower corrosion current densities and fewer localized pits. Improvements are expected under moderate to high tribological loads.
hypothesis.baseline: HEA specimens that have undergone standard post heat-treatment processing without laser shock peening.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to persist as long as the induced compressive stresses are maintained; high thermal exposures or repeated impacts that relax these stresses could nullify the advantage.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact improvement magnitudes are uncertain, given potential trade-offs between beneficial compressive stress and the creation of defects during LSP; optimal processing parameters need to be identified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical sets of HEA specimens: one set to undergo laser shock peening after heat treatment and one as a control. Perform identical tribo-corrosion tests measuring surface residual stresses (via X-ray diffraction), wear mass loss, and corrosion parameters (via potentiodynamic polarization).
measurements: XRD-based residual stress profiles
Wear volume loss measurements
Corrosion current density and potential via polarization tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser-shock-peened specimens do not show a statistically significant increase in compressive residual stress and corresponding improvements in both wear resistance and corrosion performance relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C9

source_paper.title: Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the established dynamic amorphization and inverse Hall-Petch behavior of HEAs under sliding (PMC7311485) and incorporates the known benefits of compressive residual stresses in retarding crack formation and corrosion.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a mechanical surface treatment (shot-peening) designed to introduce beneficial compressive residual stresses that preserve the ultra-nanocrystalline dynamic shear layer and reduce corrosion susceptibility—a coupling of mechanical stress engineering with tribo-corrosion performance that was not explored in the original study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Surface shot-peening induces compressive residual stresses that stabilize the ultra-nanocrystalline surface layer, reducing cavitation and crack formation, which simultaneously limits wear and stress-assisted corrosion.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Laser additive manufactured equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA with coarse grains that dynamically refine during sliding, leading to inverse Hall-Petch softening in inert environments.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a controlled shot-peening treatment to the as-fabricated HEA to introduce a near-surface layer (approximately the top 100 nm) with high compressive residual stresses.
hypothesis.conditions: Perform tribo-corrosion tests at room temperature in a mildly corrosive solution (e.g., dilute saltwater) comparing shot-peened specimens with as-fabricated samples.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A near-surface region with compressive residual stress, which both preserves the dynamically refined ultra-nanocrystalline structure during sliding and suppresses crack initiation and cavitation at grain boundaries.
hypothesis.mechanism: Shot-peening generates high compressive residual stresses in the near-surface region. These stresses retard the nucleation and propagation of microcracks as well as cavitation—phenomena that are known to exacerbate both wear and corrosion in tribological contacts. The stabilized stress field helps preserve the continuity of the ultra-nanocrystalline layer, allowing the low shear strength (and thus low friction) benefits of dynamic amorphization to persist. At the same time, the compressive stress mitigates the opening of grain boundaries, reducing the ingress of corrosive species and lowering localized corrosion rates.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated specimens, shot-peened HEA should retain a similar low friction coefficient and wear behavior driven by the inverse Hall-Petch mechanism, while exhibiting reduced corrosion current density and fewer corrosion initiation sites due to the suppression of stress-assisted grain boundary opening. The magnitude of improvement will depend on the induced compressive stress level but is expected to be significant in limiting corrosion.
hypothesis.baseline: As-fabricated HEA specimens that dynamically amorphize during sliding but lack a beneficial residual stress state, making them more susceptible to cavitation-related wear and stress-corrosion cracking under tribo-corrosion conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism will be effective if the shot-peening process is optimized to produce a thin compressively stressed layer without inducing surface roughness that might increase friction; if the peening intensity is too high, it could damage the surface or alter the grain refinement process.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact level and depth profile of compressive residual stress required to balance the benefits for dynamic amorphization and corrosion resistance is not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens—one set subjected to optimized shot-peening (with measured residual stress profile via X-ray diffraction) and one untreated set. Conduct tribo-corrosion sliding tests in a mildly corrosive environment. Characterize the near-surface microstructure via TEM to assess grain size and crack density, measure residual stress (XRD), and perform electrochemical tests along with tribological measurements of friction and wear.
measurements: Residual stress profile (XRD)
Grain size and crack/cavitation density (TEM)
Friction coefficient and wear rate (tribometry)
Corrosion parameters (electrochemical tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the shot-peened specimens do not show a statistically meaningful reduction in corrosion indicators (e.g., corrosion current density, pitting frequency) or if the dynamic amorphization-induced low friction behavior is compromised (e.g., noticeably higher friction coefficient or wear rate) relative to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: Effect of B Content on Microstructure and Properties of CrFeNiAlSi High-Entropy Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s finding that a B0.3 HEA with fine needle-like structures offered superior wear resistance and corrosion behavior.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s work by linking the microstructural control of boride morphology directly to the stability of the passive film under simultaneous mechanical and chemical attack, thereby addressing coupled tribo-corrosion rather than wear or corrosion separately.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Fine needle-like borides stabilize the passivation layer during sliding wear, thereby reducing the initiation of localized corrosion in the HEA under tribo-corrosion conditions.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A CrFeNiAlSi HEA with a multiphase microstructure that includes a BCC matrix and boride-containing secondary phases (with a tendency to coarsen at higher B levels).
hypothesis.intervention: Tailor the processing route (e.g., precise control of cooling rate and B content) to obtain a uniform, fine needle-like boride dispersion (targeting near the optimal ~0.3 B content or slightly adjusted) rather than coarse flat structures.
hypothesis.conditions: Experiments conducted under sliding wear in a 3.5 wt % NaCl solution at ambient temperature, applying controlled loads and sliding speeds.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Uniformly distributed, fine needle-like boride precipitates at grain boundaries and interfaces.
hypothesis.mechanism: The fine borides not only enhance hardness but also reinforce grain boundaries, acting as barriers to crack propagation and helping to maintain an intact passivating oxide film during wear. The preserved passive layer limits exposure of fresh metal to aggressive electrolyte, reducing localized corrosion. This synergy governs the coupled tribo-corrosion response.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in total degradation, with lower wear mass loss and reduced corrosion current density relative to samples displaying coarse boride structures, with an expected improvement of roughly 20–30% over the baseline.
hypothesis.baseline: HEA samples with coarse secondary phases (e.g., produced at higher B content resulting in thick, flat ‘noodle-like’ boride structures) exhibiting pronounced intergranular corrosion under wear.
hypothesis.boundary: This prediction holds under moderate wear loads and in corrosive environments where passivation can develop; it may fail under excessively high loads that mechanically disrupt even a reinforced passive layer.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement is uncertain and may vary with wear load and environmental conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples by adjusting cooling rates and B content to achieve fine versus coarse boride morphologies. Subject both sets to sliding tribo-corrosion testing in 3.5 wt % NaCl, and monitor the wear loss and corrosion current densities.
measurements: Wear mass loss per unit area
Potentiodynamic polarization to obtain corrosion current density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with the fine boride dispersion do not exhibit statistically lower wear and corrosion metrics (i.e., total degradation is not significantly reduced compared to the coarse structure baseline), the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C11

source_paper.title: Titanium-induced phase changes and tribological behavior in cantor-based high entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper shows that Ti additions induce phase transformations (from FCC to higher fractions of BCC and Laves phases) that affect hardness. This hypothesis extends the idea by leveraging the inherent affinity of Ti (and Cr from the alloy) to oxidize, thereby harnessing the multiphase microstructure for rapid and protective oxide formation under tribological stress.
hypotheses.what_is_new: Unlike prior reports that treated wear and corrosion separately, this hypothesis introduces a pre-oxidation step to intentionally engineer a self-healing passive film that simultaneously counters both wear and corrosion in a single mechanistic pathway.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Pre‐oxidation treatment of a Ti‐rich Cantor-type HEA produces a thin, adherent oxide film (enriched in Cr and Ti) along phase boundaries that acts as a protective barrier during sliding. This pre‐formed film reduces both mechanical wear and subsequent corrosion by minimizing damage to the underlying metal.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A mechanically alloyed, Cantor‐based HEA with elevated Ti content (x ≈ 0.75–1.00) that in its as‐sintered state contains a multiphase microstructure (FCC, BCC, and Laves phases) and displays no deliberately engineered oxide scale.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a moderate-temperature pre-oxidation heat treatment in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (e.g., 350–400 °C in air for a short duration) to form an ultrathin, continuous oxide layer on the surface.
hypothesis.conditions: Perform tribocorrosion (pin-on-disc sliding) tests in a chloride-containing aqueous solution at ambient temperature, comparing pre-oxidized samples to as-sintered, non-treated samples under identical load and sliding distance.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A uniform, nanoscale oxide film (rich in Cr- and Ti-oxides) that partially resides along phase boundaries formed during SPS and mechanical alloying, reinforcing the surface upon repeated mechanical removal.
hypothesis.mechanism: The pre-oxidation step leads to rapid formation of a protective oxide that is more adherent to the heterogeneous microstructure. During sliding, even if the oxide locally wears off, the underlying multiphase regions—with high diffusivity at phase boundaries—enable fast re-growth of the oxide. This self-healing behavior mitigates both material removal (reducing wear volume) and limits exposure of the bare metal to corrosive attack, thus coupling improved wear resistance with corrosion protection.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as-sintered alloy, the pre-oxidized HEA should display a measurable reduction in both wear rate and corrosion current density (a moderate reduction on the order of tens of percent may be expected) under identical tribocorrosion conditions.
hypothesis.baseline: The untreated HEA coating produced via SPS from mechanically alloyed powders that lacks an engineered pre-formed oxide layer.
hypothesis.boundary: This protective mechanism should hold in environments that permit moderate oxide stability (neutral to mildly aggressive electrolytes); it may fail if the environment is so aggressive that the oxide cannot stably form or at excessively high temperatures where rapid oxide spallation occurs.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal oxide thickness and its durability under cyclic wear are not fully quantified and may vary with environmental aggressiveness.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings: one set undergoes the pre-oxidation treatment (350–400 °C in air for a prescribed duration) and the other remains in the as-sintered state. Subject both to identical pin-on-disc tribocorrosion testing in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. In-situ surface analyses (e.g., XPS or Auger electron spectroscopy) should monitor the oxide film formation/re-growth dynamics during sliding.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/N·m)
Corrosion current density and impedance from electrochemical tests
Oxide film composition and thickness (via surface spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear and corrosion rates or if the oxide film does not demonstrate faster re-growth and stability compared to the untreated baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C1

source_paper.title: Self-Lubricating Tribo-Catalytic Activity of 2D High Entropy Alloy Nanoflakes.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s finding of tribocatalytic a-C formation from ethanol on HEA nanoflakes.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It extends that mechanism to propose and test a dual protective role for the a-C layer—including corrosion mitigation—by incorporating direct electrochemical measurements and controlled solvent comparisons.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Tribocatalytically generated amorphous carbon from ethanol not only reduces friction and wear but also forms a chemically inert, impermeable barrier that diminishes electrochemical corrosion on the HEA surface.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy (HEA) with a 2D nanoflake morphology similar to (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2, spray-coated on 304L stainless steel.
hypothesis.intervention: Use an ethanol-based lubricant (providing a carbon source) versus a carbon-free, inert solvent for applying the HEA, under otherwise identical tribo-corrosion conditions.
hypothesis.conditions: Conduct ball-on-disk experiments at high contact loads in a corrosive environment (e.g., humid air with a mild electrolyte or salt mist) where flash heating is present.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An in situ formed amorphous carbon (a-C) tribolayer that overlays the HEA surface.
hypothesis.mechanism: Under high contact pressures, friction-induced flash heating on the HEA initiates catalytic conversion of residual ethanol into an a-C film. This a-C layer, being chemically inert and continuous, acts as a physical barrier to both mechanical wear and corrosive species, thereby mitigating degradation. Its dual role is to smooth the sliding interface (reducing wear) and to limit the electrochemical access of corrosive agents to the metal surface (reducing corrosion).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The ethanol-based tests will exhibit a wear rate in the order of 10⁻⁹ mm³/(N·m) and lower corrosion current densities (as measured by electrochemical methods) relative to tests with a carbon-free solvent. Also, surface analysis will detect a continuous a-C layer only in the ethanol case.
hypothesis.baseline: HEA tested with a lubricant prepared using an inert, carbon-free solvent and a control test with pure ethanol without HEA, both of which do not form the protective a-C tribolayer.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective when frictional flash heating is sufficient to catalyze ethanol decomposition. It would fail in environments that are too cold or where the solvent lacks carbon species.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in corrosion current is not precisely predicted by available data.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel tribo-corrosion tests under identical loads and corrosive atmospheres using HEA coatings applied with ethanol (carbon source) versus a carbon-free solvent. Monitor wear rates via optical profilometry and assess corrosion using potentiodynamic polarization alongside surface chemical analysis (Raman, TEM/EELS) to detect the presence of an a-C layer.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/(N·m))
Corrosion current density and potential
Surface chemical identification of amorphous carbon
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant difference in wear and corrosion metrics is observed between the two cases, or if the a-C tribolayer is absent in the ethanol case, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C13

source_paper.title: Mechanical properties and water vapour corrosion behaviour of Al x CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observation in the paper that higher Al content leads to the formation of a dense alumina (Al2O3) film that protects against corrosion (PMC11304063::web::015 and PMC11304063::web::017)
hypotheses.what_is_new: It extends the finding by proposing that, under combined mechanical wear and corrosion (tribo-corrosion), a higher surface Al content can maintain protective film integrity by rapid re-passivation, thereby coupling mechanical and chemical processes in degradation.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The tribo‐corrosion response of high‑entropy alloys is governed by the dynamic balance between mechanical removal of a protective alumina film and its rapid re-passivation. In alloys with higher Al content, faster regeneration of a dense, adherent Al2O3 layer effectively retards corrosion despite wear, whereas alloys with lower Al content cannot re-establish the film as quickly under continuous wear.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An AlxCoCrFeNi high‑entropy alloy with a relatively homogeneous microstructure and a surface capable of forming a protective oxide layer.
hypothesis.intervention: Increase surface Al content (or create an Al-enriched surface layer via selective surface alloying or diffusion treatment) to enhance rapid Al2O3 re-passivation under mechanical abrasion.
hypothesis.conditions: Tribological sliding in a corrosive water/steam environment at high temperature (e.g., 900 °C) with a constant applied load that initiates both wear and oxidation.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The formation and regeneration rate of a dense and continuous Al2O3 film on the worn surface.
hypothesis.mechanism: Under sliding, mechanical wear continuously removes the protective oxide. However, a higher local Al concentration increases the alloy’s reactivity with oxygen, resulting in rapid reformation of an adherent Al2O3 film that slows down underlying metal dissolution. In alloys with lower Al, the film re-forms too slowly, leading to prolonged exposure of fresh, reactive metal and increased corrosion.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to a matched baseline with lower surface Al, the modified alloy with enhanced surface Al should exhibit lower corrosion rates (reduced electrochemical degradation markers) while maintaining similar wear rates. The total degradation (combined wear and corrosion) is predicted to decrease, with the corrosion component reduced potentially by tens of percent, although precise values are uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: An HEA with baseline Al content processed under identical tribo-corrosion conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: This prediction holds when the mechanical wear rate is moderate so that re-passivation kinetics are not completely overwhelmed; at very high wear speeds, even rapid film reforming may be insufficient.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of film reformation under synergistic wear and high-temperature conditions are not quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlxCoCrFeNi HEA samples: one with conventional bulk composition and one with an engineered Al-enriched surface (via surface alloying or diffusion treatment). Subject both to identical tribo-corrosion testing at 900 °C under controlled sliding conditions. Compare the thickness and integrity of the protective oxide film using XPS and SEM, and measure corrosion current density via electrochemical methods.
measurements: Wear rate measurements
Corrosion current density (potentiodynamic polarization)
Film thickness and continuity via XPS/SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-enriched surface does not lead to a significant decrease in corrosion rate (or if the oxide film remains non-uniform or fails to reform rapidly compared to the baseline) under identical wear conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: Study on cavitation erosion-corrosion behavior of CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 high entropy alloy in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s detailed mapping of selective phase corrosion (PMC11378927::web::010) and evidence of localized corrosion driven by compositional heterogeneity.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a compositional tuning (reducing Cu content) to directly address the micro-galvanic corrosion sites that drive the coupled tribo-corrosion process, an aspect not previously explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The coupled tribo-corrosion behavior is controlled by localized selective phase corrosion at microstructural heterogeneities, where galvanic interactions between segregated intermetallic-rich regions and the FCC matrix accelerate degradation under mechanical stress.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An as-cast CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA with pronounced phase segregation (e.g., Cu-rich dendrites and Cr-Mo rich σ and μ phases) leading to localized corrosion sites.
hypothesis.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by reducing the Cu content to suppress the formation of Cu-rich segregations, thereby producing a more homogeneous microstructure with diminished galvanic couples.
hypothesis.conditions: Tribological testing in the same 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, under cyclic mechanical loading that replicates the tribo-corrosion environment, with both the modified alloy and the original serving as direct comparisons.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A more uniform microstructure with minimized intermetallic segregation and less pronounced compositional gradients at phase boundaries.
hypothesis.mechanism: Localized corrosion is enhanced at phase boundaries where compositional disparities (e.g., Cu-rich vs. matrix) establish micro-galvanic cells. Under mechanical loading, these regions experience accelerated damage due to reduced cohesive strength and selective phase removal. By reducing Cu, the driving force for selective phase corrosion is lowered, which in turn should mitigate the synergistic interaction between mechanical wear and localized corrosion.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA with lower Cu content should exhibit reduced localized corrosion marks (verified by fewer micro-cracks and less mass loss localized at phase boundaries) and overall lower tribo-corrosion degradation compared to the baseline alloy. The total degradation rate, particularly the corrosion component, is expected to decrease.
hypothesis.baseline: The original CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 HEA with higher Cu content.
hypothesis.boundary: This prediction holds in corrosive environments where galvanic interactions due to microstructural heterogeneity are the dominant mechanism. It may fail if homogeneous wear mechanisms predominate or if Cu reduction adversely affects other protective attributes of the HEA.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The quantitative balance between reduced galvanic corrosion and possible impacts on mechanical properties due to Cu reduction is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two HEAs: one with the standard Cu content (CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1) and one with a reduced Cu concentration. Subject both to identical tribo-corrosion testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl. Use microscopic analysis to compare the extent of localized corrosion at phase boundaries and overall mass loss.
measurements: Spatially resolved corrosion damage (via SEM/EDS)
Mass loss measurements
Electrochemical noise and polarization data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reduced-Cu alloy does not show a statistically significant decrease in localized corrosion damage and overall mass loss compared to the baseline, or if new degradation modes emerge, the hypothesis is falsified.
